operations.evidence: A high-rise residential building has at least 7 storeys or is at least 18 metres high and has at least 2 residential units.
The threshold defines regulatory scope and does not establish the condition or risk level of a particular building.
A higher-risk building must be registered with the Building Safety Regulator before people live there.
Registration status is an administrative requirement and does not prove that every safety risk is controlled.
An accountable person is an organisation or individual that owns or has a legal obligation to repair common parts.
The role must be determined from ownership and repairing obligations, not inferred from a marketing or management label.
Each building must have one principal accountable person; with multiple accountable persons, the party responsible for the structure and exterior is normally the PAP.
A PAP cannot be identified without building-specific ownership and lease evidence.
Accountable persons may appoint agents to carry out duties, but their legal accountability and liability remain with them.
Use of a managing agent does not transfer statutory accountability.
A PAP organisation may name a person or third party as BSR contact, but this does not make that person or third party the PAP.
A contact record is not evidence of legal ownership or accountable-person status.
In complex leaseholds, accountable-person status follows ownership or a relevant obligation to repair or maintain common parts.
The repairing obligation must be verified from legal documents.
Where accountable persons and Fire Safety Order responsible persons differ, building safety information must be shared and data-protection requirements observed.
Information sharing does not merge the distinct statutory roles.
Accountable persons assess and manage risks from structural failure or spread of fire in the parts for which they are responsible.
A general duty does not establish that a specific hazard exists in a building.
Accountable persons must report safety occurrences, support resident engagement, keep golden-thread information and provide required building information.
The existence of these duties does not prove that each duty has been fulfilled for a named building.
Before accessing a residence to assess or manage building safety risks, an accountable person must normally request access in writing at least 48 hours in advance and explain why.
The power is conditional and does not permit unannounced entry.
Multiple accountable persons must work together and share safety information about the building.
Cooperation requirements do not remove each party's responsibility for its own parts.
For long-lease units, accountable persons must prevent risks in units affecting common parts and protect units from risks in areas they control.
This duty does not prove the presence or absence of compartmentation defects in a unit.
The PAP must submit structural and fire-safety information at registration and notify BSR of changes to submitted information.
A change notification is not evidence that the underlying change is safe or unsafe.
Accountable persons must have relevant competence or appoint competent help, and should continually monitor appointed persons' competence and capacity.
Qualifications or standards alone do not guarantee compliance with all legal duties.
Assessing how safety incidents can happen helps accountable persons understand risks, manage them and demonstrate all reasonable steps.
A risk assessment supports decisions but is not proof that an incident will occur.
A risk-assessment team should include knowledge and experience of safety management systems, fire safety and structural safety.
The listed disciplines do not by themselves demonstrate that a particular team is competent.
The assessment team does not always have to include consultants, though specialist knowledge may be needed depending on the building.
This guidance must not be used to exclude specialists where complexity requires them.
Assessments should distinguish hazards in flats from hazards in halls, community rooms, plant rooms and other areas.
Area categories are not parcel-level hazard findings.
Building risks can change during occupation and refurbishment, requiring ongoing risk management.
A refurbishment does not automatically mean risk increased or decreased.
Building safety risk assessments should consider all foreseeable scenarios relevant to the building.
The published examples are not an exhaustive checklist for every building.
Fire scenarios can include single-floor, between-floor, multiple-floor and whole-building spread.
Scenario inclusion does not establish that fire spread has occurred.
Assessments should consider failures of evacuation routes, early detection, access and other emergency-response factors.
A scenario is a planning assumption rather than an observed event.
Assessments should consider whether failure of one or more safety-system components could allow escalation.
Potential failure must not be represented as confirmed equipment failure.
Structural scenarios can include local, multiple-floor or whole-building collapse, balconies, foundations, gas explosion and impact damage.
The scenario family is not evidence of a structural defect in a named building.
Scenario planning should include worst-case outcomes, including failed controls, incorrect assumptions and escalation.
Worst-case analysis must not be presented as the most likely outcome.
Accountable persons should check that controls for which they are responsible remain effective and operate as designed.
A documented control does not prove operational effectiveness without inspection or testing evidence.
What counts as reasonable depends on building-specific circumstances, existing controls, additional measures, added risks and proportionality of cost.
Cost or inconvenience alone must not be used as a universal reason to reject a safety measure.
The Act does not mandate one assessment method; the chosen method should be fit for purpose, proportionate to complexity and cover the full range of risks.
Use of a named methodology does not guarantee a complete or correct assessment.
Accountable persons should record assessments, track actions and recommendations to completion, maintain new information and explain rejected measures.
A recorded action is not evidence that it has been completed.
A safety management system is a formal framework for managing safety risks.
The existence of a framework does not prove that controls are effective.
